Title: CORRAL Final Report
URL: http://repository.jisc.ac.uk/1386/1/corralfinalreport.pdf
Published: 2009-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
Author: Wheeler, Dennis
Highlights:
The overall strategy of the CORRAL project was two-fold; on the one hand to extract scientific data from a subset of the very large number – over 100,000 - of Royal Navy (RN) logbooks held in the National Archives at Kew and in the National Meteorological Archives (Exeter) and, on the other hand, to bring to wider public attention and make freely available images of the logbooks of the voyages of discovery. This subset enjoys the particular virtues of combining scientific observations of a very high quality and notable quantity with documents of a singular historical importance that passes far beyond the scientific and historical communities reaching out to a wider public. The written accounts provide us with a unique insight into some of the great voyages of discovery, written by those who undertook them, and their views of what were sometimes the first European encounters with hitherto unknown peoples, cultures and places. This was supplemented by the digitisation of late 19 th and early 20 th century weather observations from six Bahamian lighthouses bound in with ship logbooks and the imaging and digitisation of similar data in the ‘Climatological Returns’ from Malden Island in the Pacific Ocean and St Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean that are all held in the National Meteorological Archives and Devon Record Office in Exeter. At the time of writing this report the team have successfully imaged all 300 logbooks in the special collection of ‘voyages of discovery’ (catalogued under ADM55 in TNA) and from ships on hydrographic surveying service (ADM 53), producing over 50,000 high-quality images all of which are freely available on the BADC partner website http://badc.nerc.ac.uk/data/corral/index.html. These images are catalogued by officer, ship, period of voyage and destination(s) thereby allowing users to quickly identify those items that might be of particular interest. Weather observations from published secondary sources of some of these voyages are also available from work done under the international ACRE initiative, and have been used to supplement the primary sources when needed in the visualisations of particular voyages. Images are also available from the ‘Climatological Returns’ for Malden Island in the Pacific Ocean and St Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean. The abstracted data from registers are available (in the form of accessible MS Excel spreadsheets) on the CORRAL site at www.corral.org.uk. These data will be added to by the inclusion of those abstracted from the logbooks themselves. Although not yet freely available, the CORRAL Hadley Centre team under the international ACRE (Atmospheric Circulation Reconstructions over the Earth) (http://www.met-acre.org/) initiative have produced visualisations of the voyages plotting their routes, coloured coded as climatic conditions changed. Not only do such visualisations act as an immediate summary of the voyages but the route and progress of the vessels provide new and important information on ice cover extent and timing in Arctic regions. In addition to these achievements the team have also assembled a series of catalogues of logbooks that will serve to guide later researchers in this field. As noted above, with over 100,000 such documents for the period before 1850 alone, it is important that researchers and users can

Project Acronym: CORRAL Version: 2 Contact: Dennis Wheeler th Date: 15 October 2009 quickly identify those items that are of most importance to them. These catalogues are available on the principal CORRAL site. An overview and access to the CORRALoutputs will also be available of the RECLAIM (Recovery of Logbooks and International Marine Data) project website at http://icoads.noaa.gov/reclaim/ . This important site supported by NOAA will provide for maximum coverage of our activities within the wider remit of world-wide data recovery undertakings. The collective outcome of the project has been to provide for the needs of both the scientific and the wider communities. We have, by making the logbook images freely available, placed at the disposal of many some of our nation’s most valued and interesting documents in their original form. In conclusion the team have achieved all of the objectives described in the original project document. These being: Objective 1. To identify and catalogue all RN logbooks from before 1850 which contain instrumental weather observations. Objective 2. To create a database of instrumental climatic data derived from RN logbooks, from logbooks of vessels on voyages of scientific discovery and from colonial records. Objective 3. To create a web-based library of images of the most important logbooks from ships on voyages of scientific exploration (1700 to 1850). Objective 4. To make the instrumental database freely available to the wider scientific community through supported website ‘gateways’. Objective 5. To promote a wider interest in the large quantity of archived but hitherto unused climatic data.

...

Objective 1. To identify and catalogue all RN logbooks from before 1850 which contain instrumental weather observations. Comment: The team identified all such logbooks, these being of particular importance in scientific research and not confined to the subset of exploration logbooks and includes others from the ‘standard’ RN ships’ logbooks in collection ADM53. This document is available on the CORRAL website. Objective 2. To create a database of instrumental climatic data derived from RN logbooks, from logbooks of vessels on voyages of scientific discovery and from colonial records. It should be added however that this catalogue is confined to those RN logbooks that are archived under the National Archives ADM53 and ADM55 collections of ships’ logbooks and logbooks of voyages of discovery respectively. Comment: the task of transcribing imaged data into digital (database) form is an unavoidably lengthy one. We have completed the transcription of register (lighthouse) records and, again, these are freely available on the project website. The transcription of logbook data was more demanding and a decision was made to concentrate of the logbooks from the Arctic region; an area of great climatological significance. These data will soon be available but have been used very profitably with visualisation procedures for annotated voyage trajectory simulations. Objective 3. To create a web-based library of images of the most important logbooks from ships on voyages of scientific exploration (1700 to 1850). Comment: CORRAL now offers an image library of nearly 50,000 images from some 300 selected logbooks. We are continuing to work on a user-friendly catalogue access system, but the site is open to all and supported by our partners at BADC. The site will have ‘gateways’ through the CORRAL, the National Archives and University of Sunderland pages. We plan to extend access through other ‘portals’ and are negotiating with the Royal Meteorological Society on this point. Such material can ultimately be linked into the substantial web-based interface being developed by the international ACRE initiative. Objective 4. To make the instrumental database freely available to the wider scientific community through supported website ‘gateways’. Comment: all register-based (lighthouse) data are now available on the CORRAL site as Excel spreadsheets. When verified and completed, the data from the Arctic logbooks (see above) will be placed on the CORRAL website for equally free access. Objective 5. To promote a wider interest in the large quantity of archived but hitherto unused climatic data.

Title: Light Station Components
URL: https://web.archive.org/web/20070703130301/http:/www.nps.gov/history/maritime/ltcomp.htm
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Keeper's dwelling Second in importance to the light tower, dwellings for light keepers and their families were generally in the early days simple, 1 ½-story wooden or stone structures. Since lighthouses had only one keeper, there was only one dwelling. After 1852 with the coming of the Fresnel lens and the Lighthouse Board, more keepers began to be assigned to light stations, and, of course, it became necessary to have more living accommodations. Keeper's quarters could be single, double, triple, or even quadruple dwellings; they reflected the prevailing architectural styles, adaptations to geographical conditions, or regional tastes. Complaints by keepers concerning lack of privacy for their families finally persuaded the Lighthouse Board not to build tri-plex housing. By 1913 the U.S. Lighthouse Service stressed that "recent practice favors detached houses, insuring greater privacy, and giving better opportunity for yards and gardens." For all practical purposes, prior to 1852 there were two types of land-based lighthouses--either a detached dwelling or an integral dwelling with the light tower rising out of the roof. The early integral towers had the tower supported by the roof system. ... In colder climates, such as New England and the Great Lakes, the light tower often was either attached to the dwelling or an enclosed passageway was built between the two structures. Oil house During the early days oil was often stored in the lighthouse. As late at the early 1850s, plans for the first west coast lighthouses called for the oil storage area to be in the basement. Some lighthouse towers were constructed with attached oil room and workroom structures which were generally one-story, constructed of masonry, had gable roofs, and were modest in detailing; examples include Pensacola, Pigeon Point, and Yaquina Head Lighthouses. By 1890, all except a few lighthouses in the United States were using kerosene. The volatile nature of kerosene necessitated the construction of separate oil houses, which were usually built of fireproof materials such as brick, stone, iron plate and concrete. Congress issued a series of small appropriations for the construction of separate fireproof oil houses at each lighthouse station. Installation of these structures began in 1888 and completed about 1918. The 1902 Instructions to Light-Keepers stated: "All mineral oil belonging to the Light House Service shall be kept in an oil house or a room by itself. The oil house shall be visited daily to detect loss by leakage or otherwise, and every precaution taken for the safe keeping of the oil." Though they varied in size, lighthouses with smaller lenses had relatively small oil houses and those stations with the large lenses had relatively larger oil houses. Constructed of stone, brick, cast iron, and concrete, oil houses were small, simple, and functional, usually with a gabled or a pyramid roof. When oil was no longer required, the structures were used for other storage purposes, often paint storage.

Title: Light Station Buildings - Cape Lookout National Seashore (U.S. National Park Service)
URL: https://www.nps.gov/calo/learn/historyculture/clls-buildings.htm
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
The lighthouse was a central part of any light station, but many other structures were vital to its operation. From housing for keepers to storage for fuel, these buildings allowed for smooth operation of the lighthouse and helped ensure that the beacon would be ready to warn mariners away from dangerous waters.

...

#### First Keeper's Quarters (1812) - Destroyed

This Keeper's Quarters was built at the same time as the first Cape Lookout lighthouse. The letter calling for proposals detailed the specifications for this house. The house was to be 24 feet by 24 feet and one and a half stories tall. Each of the three rooms had a fireplace which fed into the chimney in the center of the house. The exterior was made of pine and covered with pine or cedar shingles. In 1869, this house received extensive repairs.

A kitchen was to be built at least 6 feet away from the house and connected with covered walkway. The proposal request indicated that this kitchen should be 14 feet by 16feet and one-story tall. A well was also part of this request.

It is unknown how long these structures remained standing. Photographic records indicate that the Keeper's Quarters remained standing at least until 1893. Part of the foundation of this dwelling can be seen on a sand dune in the lighthouse area.

#### Second Keeper's Quarters (1873)

Soon after the second Cape Lookout lighthouse was completed, Assistant Keepers were assigned to the station. A new Keepers' Quarters was built in 1873 to accommodate these keepers. The house was designed as a single-family residence, but by the early 1900s, all three keepers were living in this building. In response to complaints that their families could not be with them, a new Head Keeper's Quarters was built in 1907. The two Assistant Keepers and their families then shared the 1873 dwelling.

Today, this Keepers' Quarters serves as a museum, giving visitors a glimpse into the lives of Lighthouse Keepers and Surfmen of the US Life-Saving Service. The museum is open from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, seven days a week during the spring, summer, and fall.

#### Third Keeper's Quarters (1907) - Moved

In response to a need for more housing, this Keeper's Quarters was built in 1907. It housed the primary Keeper and his family from the fall of 1907 until the tower was automated in 1950. Although the house is brown today, it was white washed in historic photos.

In 1957, the house was deemed surplus and sold to Dr. Graham Barden, Jr., which is why it is also called the Barden House. Barden moved the house 1.1 miles southwest of the lighthouse to the Cape Lookout Village using a "low-boy trailer with a bulldozer behind and a caterpillar tractor pulling in front." This building is currently closed to the public.

...

#### Oil House (circa 1930s or 1940s)

Oil couldn't be stored in the lighthouse, because the lighthouse required a large amount of oil to keep it burning. A single spark could ignite a fire or explosion. This concrete oil house replaced an iron structure that was built in 1897.

The building is open today, but visitors should use caution when entering the shed as the floor is uneven and may contain debris from the structure.

## The keeper's dwelling

The dwelling is a two-storey rectangular brick house with a steep gabled roof, attached directly to the tower. It belongs to a plan sometimes called the schoolhouse type, from the resemblance: a plain, well-proportioned domestic block with the tower rising at one end rather than out of the centre of the roof.

The attachment matters more than it looks. On this coast a keeper had to reach the lantern in February, in the dark, in a gale, with ice on everything. A detached tower means going outside to do it. An attached tower means a door. The whole northern Great Lakes family of station plans is organised around that single problem, and the 1869 rebuilding took the opportunity to solve it here.

A long covered porch runs across the lake side of the house. Its use is not primarily scenic: on an exposed shore a porch is a buffer, keeping driven snow and spray off the door and the wall behind it, and giving somewhere to leave wet gear.

## The oil house

Plate III The oil house: small, thick-walled, deliberately detached.

The small brick oil house is the most easily overlooked building on the site and the one that best explains how the station worked. Before electrification a light burned fuel — first sperm oil, later lard oil, then mineral oil — and the station had to keep a working stock of it on hand through a shipping season that closed with the ice.

Storing that much combustible liquid inside a dwelling where a family slept was an obvious risk, and after a run of fires across the service the Lighthouse Board standardised on exactly this solution: a small, thick-walled, single-purpose structure set apart from everything else, with a heavy door and minimal openings. Its detachment from the house is the entire point of it. The former owners recorded that this one survives in good condition.

<tool_result source="call_j34fd76y55hpsj6npvyutk0g" state="ok">Title: The Lighthouse Keeper’s Lantern Pane Duties – Maine Lights Today
URL: https://www.mainelightstoday.com/lighthouse-keepers-lantern-pane-duties/
Published: 2022-01-04T02:38:32.000Z
Author: Bob Trapani, Jr.
Highlights:
Looking back through lighthouse history, you might say that keepers were very good at cleaning windows. Maybe not by choice, but duty called nonetheless. When it came to the panes of a lantern, keepers were instructed to diligently remove any dirt, soot, condensation, frost, ice or drift snow that might accumulate upon the surface of the glass during the light’s hours of operation. This included both the interior and exterior panes.

According to the 1870 United States Light-House Board Instructions and Directions to Guide Light-House Keepers and Others Belonging to the Light-House Establishment, “The plate glass of the lantern must be kept at all times during the exhibition of the lights entirely free from dampness or moisture by frequently wiping it off both outside and inside with clean, dry towels.”

...

Light stations with more than one keeper often fared better than stations with one keeper during such stormy times. Under the heading of “Cleaning the snow, ice, frost &c., from the plate-glass” in the 1870 instructions, the Light-House Board stated, “For the more effectual removal of snow, ice frost and wet from the plate-glass of the lantern, which may have accumulated in the day, during the winter period, from October 1 to March 31, two keepers must go and remain on watch throughout the first hour, from half an hour before until half an hour after sunset, one to perform all the duties connected with the apparatus, lighting the lamp, regulating the height of the flame, the damper and ventilation; the other to remove the apparatus cover, take down the lantern curtains, and return the oil carriers and other utensils to their proper places, &c.”

...

The instructions went on to say, “The journal of the light station must show that these double watches are regularly kept from October 1 to March 31, and by whom, on each day during that period of time. The keepers in charge of the lights, after the expiration of the double watch, are required to remove all accumulations of drift snow, sleet, ice, and frost from the outside, and to remove all moisture that accumulates on the inside of the glass of the lantern.”

As challenging as fast-accumulating snow or sleet upon lantern panes could be, the most dreaded obstruction was freezing rain. The instant freeze of the falling rain upon cold glass surfaces could create an opaque crisis real quick for keepers. Clearing any thickness of ice from the panes was not only a tough job, but rarely was the cleaning process initially uniform. Scraping the same area over a number of times to remove stray streaks of ice could easily be required. In addition, the keeper also had to be mindful of not cracking the glass panes as he worked to clear the icy obstructions.

...

According to the 1870 instructions, “When ice, sleet, or drift-snow settles on the outside, or when the ice forms in cold weather on the inside of the glass of the lantern, a strong brine applied to it will remove it without difficulty, and, in extreme cases, a small quantity of spirits of wine may be employed with advantage for the same purpose.”

Highlights:
The lamp itself needed coaxing into life. Most lighthouses of the period burned colza, spermaceti or, later in the century, paraffin in an Argand-type burner, with a hollow wick that drew air up through the middle of the flame. The keeper trimmed that wick with scissors until the top was even and the flame burned white rather than smoky, then wiped every pane of the lantern glass, polished the brasswork and cleaned the soot from the chimney above the flame. A smeared pane or a charred wick could cut the range of the light by miles.

...

At sunrise the light was extinguished and the real work began. By day a lighthouse is a building exposed to salt, damp and wind, and it loses that fight continuously.

- Cleaning the lens and lantern panes with soft cloths and spirit, never anything abrasive.
- Trimming and replacing wicks, filling and cleaning the oil reservoirs, filtering oil.
- Polishing brass and copper, blackleading the stove, sweeping and scrubbing the tower stairs.
- Painting and whitewashing — an annual ritual that swallowed weeks of fine weather.
- Hauling coal, water, provisions and oil up from the landing place.
- Tending the garden, feeding the chickens or goat, catching rain in the cistern for washing.
- Recording weather, temperature and barometer readings in the log.

Title: Fresnel Lens Care Guidelines
URL: https://uslhs.org/sites/default/files/attached-files/Fresnel%20Lens%20Care%20Guidelines.pdf
Published: N/A
Author: Thomas Tag
Highlights:
• To protect against harmful Ultra Violet rays of the sun, use historically correct shades, curtains or lens covers and/or where possible, UV rated film on lantern room windows. Minimum UV protective rating required is 99%. (UV rate film must meet the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for the treatment of historic properties.) 
• The lantern room is to be kept clean and clear of debris, and in good repair. At a minimum, there should be no roof leaks, lantern windows need to be kept properly glazed and caulked to protect against air and water intrusion. Floor, wall, and roof vents should be kept clean and free of accumulations of dirt, insects, birds or their nests. Cleaning tools, stools, ladders, etc. will not be stored in the lantern room. 
• Access to lantern room by visitors shall be supervised at all times by authorized personnel (trained docents or staff). Visitors shall be prohibited from touching or coming into contact with any part of the lens, such as touching with hands or bumping with camera equipment. 
• The size of the lantern room shall be used in determining the number of visitors allowed inside at any one time in order to prevent overcrowding and possible damage to the Fresnel lens. The number of visitors allowed at one time shall not exceed six persons and may be less depending on the situation. 
• An initial baseline condition assessment of a Fresnel lens following its transfer from the Coast Guard to the new owner is a necessary starting point from which to measure its condition through time. Therefore, this initial assessment shall be conducted in situ by a professional lampist (see list) or a professional artifact conservator (AIC affiliated) within six months after the Fresnel lens is transferred. The lampist or conservator shall prepare a written report and file a copy with the Coast Guard Curator’s office not later than one month following this assessment. Additional condition assessments by a professional lampist/conservator with written reports shall be conducted at intervals of not more than six years thereafter,

...

## Standard care, maintenance, and cleaning methods

• Bi-weekly to monthly visual checks on prism glass and metal framework. Polishing of metalwork is prohibited due to erosion of metal. 
• If the lens appears to be in good condition and maintained within recommended parameters, minimal contact is considered best practice for long term preservation and damage control. 
• Staff should be trained initially by a qualified individual familiar with the proper care and maintenance of Classical Fresnel lenses. 
• As needed light dusting of glass and metal parts with a microfiber cloth or soft microfiber duster 
• Remove all jewelry, watches and belt buckles prior to cleaning. 
• Use of nitrile or soft cotton gloves required when cleaning the lens. 
• To wet-clean dirty glass: combine 2 parts distilled water to 1 part isopropyl alcohol. Add only one drop of original, non-concentrated Woolite per quart of distilled water/isopropyl alcohol mixture. To wipe: dampen cloth and gently wipe from side to side, and wipe dry with dry cloth. Use a clean microfiber rag. Do not spray cleaning solution directly onto glass. 
• STRICTLY PROHIBITED products: sandpaper, Brillo pad, Brasso, Windex or ammonia products. No abrasive or corrosive cleaning and polishing products.

## Cleaning Without Doing Harm

Glass in a marine environment collects a film of salt, dust and organic matter that dulls the light and, over time, etches the surface. Clean regularly but gently. Warm water with a little pH-neutral detergent and a soft cloth or sponge is almost always the right answer. Avoid abrasive pads and strong acidic cleaners, which can attack both the glass and the metal frame and leave the surface more prone to future staining.

Rinse thoroughly with fresh water afterwards, because leaving detergent residue behind simply attracts more dirt. In coastal locations, a final rinse with clean water is worth more than any polishing. Where heritage glass is original and slightly wavy or tinted, treat it with extra care; replacement in matching style can be difficult and expensive, so preserving what is there is always the first aim.

...

According to some interviewees, lighthouse families’ attitudes towards nature were ‘rather healthy’. Austerity and nativeness of materials and techniques in Greek lighthouses construction have rendered them eco-friendly and compatible with their natural surroundings anyway; they seem to cause no rupture or intrusion into land or seascapes. ##### The Sea Serpant

Local Indigenous legends warned early settlers of a large serpent-like creature living off West Point, a being that has reportedly been sighted for over two centuries, including as recently as 1992 and 2002. Descriptions vary, but witnesses often report a long, dark, hair-covered, snake-like animal with multiple visible humps and a horse-like head rising above the water as it moves quickly and sometimes submerges for long periods. Similar accounts of large sea serpents have been recorded in other North American lakes and coastal areas, with many describing nearly identical features and movements. While skeptics doubt its existence, those who claim to have seen it describe a striking and unforgettable creature that continues to fuel local mystery and legend.

Sea Phantoms

##### The Flaming Vessel

The flaming ship of West Point, PEI, is a well- known tale that has been passed down through generations. It is said to be a 

ghostly ship that has been spotted sailing along the coast, often accompanied by flames. The story goes that a group of sailors once encountered this ship, which was seen with white sails and flames. As they 

approached, they heard screams of panic and watched as the ship's masts were climbed frantically. The sailors jumped into a rowboat to chase the ship, which then vanished without a trace, leaving no signs of its whereabouts. This tale is so prevalent that it is even taught to children as part ofthe island's history. The flaming ship is a testament to the island's rich maritime heritage and the stories that have shaped its identity

##### Keepers of the Light

During the early years of the West Point Lighthouse Inn, volunteers often stayed overnight and occasionally experienced unexplained events involving the building’s lights. On one occasion in the 1980s, a volunteer repeatedly turned off an upstairs light only to find it mysteriously back on moments later, eventually leaving the building. In another incident after renovations, volunteers shut off all power before leaving, yet returned to find kitchen lights turned on despite the switches and breaker being off. With no explanation found for these occurrences, staff came to jokingly attribute them to the former lighthouse keepers, suggesting the “old keepers” may still be watching over and tending to the light.

Early settlers in West Point, mainly from Scotland and Ireland, brought with them strong beliefs in folklore and the supernatural, including witches, pixies, and other mystical forces. Here, we're dealing mostly with two myths in particular, the Greek figures of Proteus and Prometheus.

"[W]e realized, 'Well, Prometheus and Proteus never hung out in any Greek myths before, but that seems to be what is kind of happening here,' and Prometheus might be taking on some characteristics that he hasn’t in the past," Eggers said in that same interview. Proteus was one of myth's first old men of the sea, a primordial keeper of knowledge and friend to the sea-beasts that knew everything there is to know but hated sharing that knowledge, prickly old shithead that he was. Prometheus, on the other hand, was one heck of a giver; a trickster Titan, Prometheus famously stole fire from the gods, sparking intelligent life in humanity. Zeus, a noted asshole all around, ordered Prometheus chained to a rock, where an eagle would arrive every day to pick out the Titan's organs.

...

The Lighthouse combines mythology and mood to tell a story about people who don't understand themselves. Like the fire Prometheus nabbed from the gods, the light at the top of the tower represents everything, all knowledge, and in looking into it Thomas understood everything, all at once. The sea itself has played a considerable role in developing humans as a species but traveling the waters in the early ages was riskier than going into outer space today. Hence, a mariner's life was full of superstitions. Even today, any expedition based on chance or luck is predisposed to superstitions. Most of these superstitions that rose at sea were usually contrived beliefs and rituals that sailors relied on to give them hope that they will have a better chance at sea. The maritime museum in New Zealand listed some weird superstitions; for example, bananas were believed to be so unlucky they would cause the ship to be lost, or some words and sayings brought bad luck on board, including "drowned," "goodbye" and "good luck." Even mentioning things that were related to land were believed to invite bad luck. Birds were thought to carry dead sailors' souls, so killing a gull or an albatross brought bad luck. Throwing stones into the sea was known to cause storms, and huge swells and whistling was supposed to get a calm breeze. The ancient Egyptians used to paint eyes on the bow to help the ship find its way. Sailors also heard strange sounds at sea, usually thought to be blamed on sirens or mermaids who sang enchanted songs. These "melodies" lured sailors towards land, causing them to crash into underlying rocks. There have been so many of these superstitions that were born from 4 being lost at sea with no sign of hope. As the technology evolved, these superstitions reduced in number because the sea was getting much more comfortable to travel through. The technological advancements in navigation also reduced the risk of shipwrecks and reduced the fear in sailors.

The figures indicate that in the 1880s and 1890s the German flag held a respectable second place in Hong Kong's shipping statistics even though still lagging far behind the British flag. As Table 1 has demonstrated, most vessels entering and clearing the port were employed in coastal and short-sea shipping on the China coast and in the neighbouring N anyang. These destinations were also the main field of operation for German tramps but with a clear and distinct division between North and South China. As a contemporary observer in the spring of 1894 noted, German shipping had left the coastal trade north of Hong Kong almost entirely in British, Chinese and Japanese hands. Indeed, the three major shipping companies - China Navigation Company, Inda-China Steam Navigation Company, and China Merchants - dominated the Northern China shipping market leaving only bulk freight such as beans, peas, and bean cake to German vessels sailing from China's most northern port, Newchwang, via Chefoo to Hong Kong and Canton. The sheer amount Coastal Shipping in East Asia in the Late Nineteenth Century 279 of available cargo in such bulk products still provided German coasters with a considerable share of this trade despite growing Japanese competition on the main shipping routes between China, Japan and Korea. 119 Jebsen's letters indicate that his vessels Doris and]acob Diederichsen were frequently employed in the Newchwang trade during 1894. 120 These direct shipments in bulk goods from North to South China were the last remaining niche for German shipping in the Northern Chinese market. The situation did not change appreciably until the First World War, a situation which was often complained about in official statements from German diplomatic and consular staff in China. 12 1 It therefore became a matter of national prestige to have a regular line under the German flag in North China, something that was finally achieved in 1898 with the highly-subsidised postal steamer service between Shanghai, Kiaochow, Chefoo and Taku (Tientsin), initially operated by Jebsen but from 1901 to 1914 by the Hamburg-Amerika Line. 122 Beyond North China the Jebsen coasters sailed to ports in Russian Asia and regularly plied the Siberian coast so that his shipmasters knew these waters quite well. Voyages in time charter to this region usually began and ended in Hong Kong, and it was common practice for trips north of Vladivostok that an extra amount of 3,000 dollars on top of the agreed freight rate was charged. Generally the charter contracts permitted trips to Sakhalin Island and the Kamchatka peninsula but excluded the Amur district for which, due to the difficult and dangerous navigation on the river, an extra premium of around 4,000 to 6,000 marks had to be paid .123 On the return voyage these vessels often called at the Japanese port of Nagasaki , then Newchwang and Chefoo in search of suitable cargo. 124 The main field of operation for German and other tramps was the region west and south of Hong Kong, namely the waters around Hainan Island, the Gulf of Tonkin, and the Nanyang. Jebsen's letters indicate that his coasters frequently serviced the route between Hong Kong, Haihow, Pakhoi and Haiphong, French Indochina, and even further south to Touran, Saigon, Bangkok, Singapore, and Manila. The main reason for the strong position of tramps in this region was the fact that these ports, with the exception of the British colony of Singapore, exported only agricultural bulk commodities. Since the freight market was entirely dependent on the result of harvests it proved to be a high-risk venture for shipping companies to launch regular services to such destinations . On the other hand tramp ships found an almost perfect situation to compete in this market. 125 280 Bert Becker Already in the mid-1890s, however, contemporary observers foresaw that sooner or later such permanent shipping services would eventually be established because commerce and shipping capacities in East Asia were rapidly increasing. 126 This optimism is present in a letter from Jebsen who, at the beginning of 1890, just before the new depression began, seriously considered establishing a regu lar shipping service in the Nanyang . Earlier Behn & Meyer of Singapore had approached him with the idea of establishing one regular service between Singapore and Bangkok, providing feeder services for the transcontinental steamers of North German Lloyd, the major German shipping company at the time. They also wanted to launch another service between Singapore and Borneo. 'It seems that even if such services are not initially profitable they should prove to be good in the course of time and offer many advantages compared to irregular voyages during periods when markets are weak', Jebsen wrote. 127 However, the depression of the early 1890s certainly brought an end to this idea and there are no further remarks on the matter in Jebsen's letters. Only after the launch of Jebsen & Co in Hong Kong by Jebsen's son Jacob and a partner in March 1895 was a regular service established between Hong Kong and ports further west, namely Hoihow on Hainan Island and Pakhoi, wi th occasional voyages to Haiphong, the major port of northern French Indochina. 128 On the return voyages from Hoihow the cargo usually consisted mainly of pigs while from Haiphong large quantities of rice were shipped back to Hong Kong. Four or five ofJebsen's coasters serviced this route which became one of the backbones of the shipping company until the outbreak of the First World War. 129 Coolie shipments from China to the Nanyang were another lucrative field of business for tramps. Several factors contributed to the mass emigration of poor Chinese labourers to a number of worldwide destinations, and this development reached a peak in the third quarter of the nineteenth century. The recruitment of coolies, often using questionable methods and involving maltreatment, was organised by Chinese brokets who also arranged shipment from Hong Kong and treaty ports such as Amoy, Swatow, and Hoihow. From these major transition ports relatively inexpensive steamship routes were important to increase and channel the flows of Chinese migrants who came mainly from particular parts of Fujian and Guahgdong provinces. The continued migration helped Western companies operating , chartering, and provisioning ships to share in the profits generated by this trade in human labour. 13° Coastal Shipping in East Asia in the Late N ineteenth Century 281 It seems that transport of coolies from Hong Kong to the United States, South America, Australia, and other faraway destinations was mainly in the hands of British, American, and French shipping firms which registered great profits . 13 1 However, in coolie shipments from Amoy and Swarow German vessels had a considerable share. In 1894 a German shipmaster reported in Hansa that the Chinese agents in Amoy had chartered one or two German steamers for passenger transport to Singapore and Penang, and that at Swatow a German company made use of a number of German steamers for coolie shipments to Sumatra in the Dutch East Indies . 132 These East Asian ports were indeed the prirne destinations for most of the Chinese migrants in the late nineteenth cedtury. Most of them went to Singapore, the biggest 'coolie market ' in East Asi ~ which was both a transhipment hub and a free trade entrepot strong~y attracting the Chinese al ready living in the Nanyang. From there migrants usually sailed to other Southeast Asian countries, namely to the Malayan peninsula, French Indochina and Siam. 133 At Singapore the German firm of Rautenberg , Schmidt & Co was the principal broker for Chinese charterers and the J ebsen coasters employed for coolie shipments. One of the Jebsen vessels especially designed for coolies was the Rio, a 1,7 36- ton passenger ship which had been used for shipping European emigrants to South America before being purchased by J ebsen in March 1891. Coolie shipments in the Rio started in the autumn of 1893 and in the following year this ship frequently sailed between Amoy and Singapore. 134 This very profitable time charter for 5,700 dollars per month was a far g reater amount than could be obtained from normal freight rates paid for the shipment of bulk goods at the time . This fact pleased J ebsen so much that he expressed the hope that 'the charterer will employ this steam er, so well suited for coolie shipping, for a longer period of time'.

Highlights:
Coastal Shipping and the Establishment of a Coastal Shipping Industry Through the formation of Nippon Yusen and Osaka Shosen, referred to as shasen (i.e. companies using their own ships), and other shipping corporations, or shagaisen (companies using outside ships), the base for Japan's maritime shipping industry was almost complete by the 1890s. However, these companies were involved in domestic shipping only. The only scheduled overseas shipping route was the one to Shanghai that the government-protected Misubishi Company had taken in 1875, and its development lagged far behind that of domestic routes. The major reason for this backwardness was that the shipping companies had not accumulated adequate capital to increase their number of ships. Nippon Yusen was the first to begin an overseas route, in March 1889, from Shanghai to Vladivostok. Osaka Shosen followed in July 1890 by putting ships on the route between Osaka and Pusan. In December, Nippon Yusen began its route between Kobe and Manila. In March 1893, Osaka Shosen began shipping between Osaka and Inchon. Shipping companies thus gradually started overseas routes to neighbouring Korea and China. Also in 1893, Nippon Yusen began Japan's first long-distance overseas route, to Bombay. Ship ownership in Japan in 1893 amounted to 680 steam vessels (110,205 tons) and 749 sailing-vessels (44,967 tons), but only 60 steam and 4 sailing-vessels were of 500 tons or more. From the size of these crafts, we can see that most were ships for inland and coastal shipping, with only a few suited to overseas routes.1 Effects of the Sino-Japanese War At the outbreak of the Sino-Japanese War in August 1894, the government commandeered almost all vessels registered by domestic shipowners for military and naval transport and purchased 14 steamships (40,000 tons) from abroad that it lent to Nippon Yusen. Nippon Yusen itself purchased 23 steamships (65,000 tons) from overseas that it used for military transport. The commandeering and procurement of 140 ships (227,000 tons) during the war impoverished merchant shipping and brought coastal shipping to a standstill.2 It was this situation that forced Naikoku Tsuun to send employees to Hokkaido and Tohoku in October 1894 to convince freight shippers to transfer their cargo from coastal to land transport. Owners of shasen and shagaisen companies tried to deal with the reduced numbers by purchasing and chartering foreign vessels or building new ships. Consequently the number of foreign-purchased ships rose rapidly from an annual 10 or fewer (8,000 ton level) at the end of 1893 to 38 (over 60,000 tons) in 1894, 35 (over 43,000 tons) in 1895, and 27 ships (over 22,000 tons) in 1896. There was also a dramatic increase in the number of shipbuilding sites, from 53 in 1894 to 82 in 1895, and a boom in the construction of steamships and sailing-ships in these years: 68 steamships (over 3,800 tons) built in 1894; 87 (over 8,400 tons) in 1895; 99 (over 6,700 tons) in 1896; and 86 sailing-ships (over 3,800 tons) in 1896; 66 (over 4,300 tons) in 1897; and 113 (over 9,700 tons) in 1898.3 This brought the number of Japanese ships registered to 1,032 (438,779 tons) steamships and 715 (48,130 tons) sailing-ships in 1897, 1.5 times the number for 1893, which also increased the registered tonnage by 400 per cent. Although the number of sailing-ships declined by 34, tonnage increased by 3,000 for an approximate 7 per cent increase overall. Two reasons for this dramatic increase in ship numbers were the 1894－1895 Sino-Japanese War and the 1896 government grants-in-aid to develop maritime companies. The grants-in-aid were based on the stipulations of one law on ocean navigation and another to encourage shipbuilding.4 The two laws were concerned primarily with ocean-going steamships of 700－1,000 tons or more; inland shipping was not under their purview. However, inland shipping was subject to a shipping inspection law enacted in amendment to these two laws that required the inspection of Japanese-type sailing-ships of 200 koku (1 koku = 180 litres) capacity or greater. In order to get around the inspection law, however, the capacity ratings for Japanese-type sailing-vessels were converted to tons, which thus gave these so-called hybrid ships (ainokosen) the advantage possessed by Western-type sailing-ships. The result was an increase in sailing-ships from 715 (over 48,000 tons) in 1897 to 1,914 (about 17,900 tons) in 1898. This brings into clear relief the number of sailing-ships operating as a part of inland shipping. The 1898 increase was due not only to converting ship capacities to tons; there were 113 (9,754 tons) ships constructed in that year, making this the largest increase in number of ships in the post-Sino-Japanese-War period. Clearly, conditions for inland shipping were favourable during this period. Table 4. Number of inland steamships and sailing-vessels (1888－1909) Favoured by the Sino-Japanese War and the law to encourage ocean navigation and shipping, both the inland and high-seas shipping industries progressed dramatically during this period, opening routes to Europe, America, and Australia.

Highlights:
그러므로 생산지나 집산지에서 직송하는 직무역이 절대적으로 유리하다. 개항 초 공히 중계무역을 통해 한국시장 진출을 노렸던 日商과 華商의 경쟁관계에서 운송망 확충은 무엇보다도 중요하였다. 화상이 단시간에 한국 무역시장에서 힘을 발휘할 수 있었던 것은 한국에서의 정치적, 경제적 세력 확대를 통해 그간 형식에 불과하였던 ‘종주권’을 강화하려는 중국 정부의 정책변화에 힘입은 바가 컸다. 중국 정부의 지원 아래 한중 간 해상운송망이 확충된 것은 화상의 상무진흥에 결정적으로 작용하였다. 한국의 내정과 외교에 깊숙이 개입하였던 袁世凱는 경제세력 확장에도 많은 관심을 기울였다. 그는 재임기간 화상의 정상적인 무역활동은 물론이고 ‘밀무역’까지도 방조하고 조장하는 등 화상의 경제활동에 유무형의 도움을 주었다. 화상의 경제진출지원 방면에서 가장 두드러지는 부분이 초상국 선박의 정기적인 한국운항을 성사시킨 것이다. 上海와 仁川을 잇는 해상운송망 확충은 화상의 무역활동을 이루는 근간이라는 경제적 의미를 지닌다. 한중항로는 운항 후 계속되는 적자에 한 차례 운항이 중단되기도 하였다. 그럼에도 항로를 재개설하고 적자상태에서도 유지한 것은 ‘상국으로서의 체면’을 중시한 李鴻章의 의지가 반영된 것이다. 이는 한중항로 개통과 유지가 정치적 의미까지 가지고 있었음을 보여주는 예이다.
